newsitem.title: USA: U.S. factories slower but still busy, spending rises.
newsitem.headline: U.S. factories slower but still busy, spending rises.

text.p: Manufacturing grew at a slightly slower rate in April and consumer spending rose in March, reports said Thursday, though there was scant evidence the economy was slowing from its torrid first-quarter pace.

The reports, along with another of a jump in new claims for jobless benefits, were probably not enough to deter Federal Reserve policy-makers from raising interest rates again later this month, analysts said.

The nation's purchasing managers said their closely watched index of manufacturing fell to 54.2 in April from 55.0 in March. A reading above 50 means growth while one below that points to contraction in manufacturing, which accounts for about 20 percent of the nation's economy.
Price pressures were muted, the National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) said in its report, the first broad look at the economy's performance in the second quarter.

The Commerce Department said in a separate report that personal incomes rose 0.6 percent in March and consumer spending rose 0.5 percent -- figures that were largely already reflected in Wednesday's report on first-quarter activity.
The government said on Wednesday that gross domestic product grew at a 5.6 percent annual rate in the first quarter, the fastest pace in more than nine years.

Consumer spending fuels two-thirds of the economy and is closely watched by economists, who said the latest reports did not settle the issue of whether the economy was slowing enough to avert another increase in rates by the Fed.

"These numbers fail to answer the question of whether the economy will slow down enough to discourage the Fed from raising interest rates further," said Jerry Jasinowski, president of the National Association of Manufacturers.

David Orr, chief economist for First Union Corp. in Charlotte, N.C., said the purchasing managers report "confirms that the momentum of the manufacturing sector remains very firm" and said it pointed to another rate increase by the Fed.

The Fed raised short-term interest rates a quarter point on March 25 in a bid to slow demand and curb inflation. The central bank's policy-makers meet again on May 20 to weigh their next move on rates, and most analysts expect another rate rise given the rapid growth in the first quarter.

While price pressures have so far remained muted, Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan has said the central bank is moving to try to prevent the economy from overheating and forcing wages and prices into an upward spiral.

A separate report from the Labour Department said that new applications for jobless benefits jumped 28,000 to 347,000 in the week ended April 26. The four-week average of new claims -- considered a more accurate gauge of the job market than the more-volatile weekly numbers -- rose to 330,500 from 321,750.
The rise may mean demand for workers was easing in tight labour markets, though new claims were boosted by one-time factors.
"The report provides tentative evidence that the job market may be cooling off," said economist Tim O'Neill of Harris Bank/Bank of Montreal in Chicago.
"But caution is warranted because part of the rise in jobless claims reflects the impact of strikes in the auto sector and floods in the Midwest," O'Neill added.
Large parts of Grand Forks and its sister city East Grand Forks, N.D., were submerged by the swollen Red River last month while workers have struck Chrysler Corp. and General Motors Corp.

A separate Commerce Department report said construction spending fell 0.2 percent in March to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $600.1 billion, but that barely made a dent in February's 2.1 percent increase.

Analysts expect the economy to slow in the second quarter as companies throttle back on production. A surge in production that helped fatten inventories contributed to the economy's sharp acceleration in the first quarter.
The NAPM index did not suggest any immediate slowing, though it was encouraging on prices. NAPM's price index fell to 49.6 from 50.9 as commodities bought by manufacturers became cheaper.

"I think it would be premature to call that (drop in the overall index) a trend," said Norbert Ore, who heads the Tempe, Ariz.-based group's monthly survey. "Our members continue to indicate that there is strength in their markets."
The personal spending report showed that despite spending more in March, consumers boosted savings to 5.3 cents of each dollar earned from 5.2 cents in February.
